rewritten_text:
“Good gracious!” thought the Duchess. “So he is a kind of cheiropodist, after all. How dreadful! I do hope he is foreign, at least. That would make it rather less bad.”

“I really must present him to you.”

“Present him!” the Duchess exclaimed. “Surely you don't mean he is here?” She began searching for her little tortoise-shell fan and a much-frayed lace shawl, preparing to depart at an instant's warning.

“Naturally he is here. I should never think of holding a party without him. He says my hand is purely psychic, and that had my thumb been the tiniest fraction shorter, I should have become a settled pessimist and entered a convent.”

“Oh, I understand!” said the Duchess, considerably relieved. “He reads fortunes, then?”

“And misfortunes as well,” Lady Windermere replied. “As many as you please. For example, next year I am threatened with great danger on both land and water, so I intend to reside in a balloon and haul my dinner up in a basket every night. It is all recorded on my little finger—or perhaps my palm; I forget.”

“But surely, Gladys, that would be tempting Providence.”

“My dear Duchess, by now Providence ought to be able to withstand temptation. I believe everyone should have their hands read monthly, to learn what they must avoid. Of course they do it nevertheless, but a warning is so agreeable. Now, unless someone fetches Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall be obliged to fetch him myself.”

“Allow me, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, good-looking young man who had been listening nearby with an entertained smile.

“Many thanks, Lord Arthur, but I fear you would not know him.”

“If he is so remarkable as you say, Lady Windermere, I could scarcely overlook him. Describe him, and I shall bring him directly.”

“Well, he looks nothing at all like a cheiromantist. That is, there is nothing mysterious, esoteric, or romantic in his appearance. He is short and stout, with an amusing bald head and enormous gold-rimmed spectacles, halfway between a family physician and a provincial attorney. I am truly sorry, but you cannot blame me. People are dreadfully irritating. Every pianist I know looks like a poet, and every poet like a pianist. Last season, I remember inviting a most terrible conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up any number of people, habitually wore chain mail, and kept a dagger up his sleeve. Yet when he arrived, do you know, he looked exactly like a kindly old clergyman and spent the entire evening making jokes?

Mr. Wickham found the conversation so entirely satisfactory that he never again troubled himself, or irritated his dear sister Elizabeth, by returning to its subject. She was glad to discover that her words had been sufficient to silence him.

Soon the day arrived for him and Lydia to leave. Mrs. Bennet had to resign herself to a separation likely to last at least a year, since her husband would have nothing to do with her proposal that they should all travel to Newcastle.

“Oh, my darling Lydia,” she exclaimed, “when shall I see you again?”

“Oh, goodness! How should I know? Perhaps not for two or three years.”

“Write very frequently, my dear.”

“As often as I am able. But married women never have much leisure for letters, you know. My sisters can write to me; they'll have nothing else to occupy them.”

Mr. Wickham took leave with far more warmth than his wife. He smiled, displayed his good looks, and offered a quantity of graceful speeches.

“He is as excellent a fellow as I ever encountered,” Mr. Bennet remarked once they had left. “He simpers and smirks and courts every one of us. I am immensely proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to furnish a more precious son-in-law.”

For several days the departure of her daughter left Mrs. Bennet very low.

“I frequently think,” she said, “that nothing is worse than separation from one's friends. Without them one feels quite deserted.”

“You see, ma'am, that is what comes of marrying off a daughter,” Elizabeth replied. “It ought to reconcile you to the other four remaining single.”

“Nothing of the kind. Lydia is not leaving because she is married, but because her husband's regiment happens to be stationed so far away. Had it been closer, she would not have left so soon.”

The melancholy into which this event had cast her was soon dispelled, however. A piece of news beginning to circulate reopened her mind to all the excitement of hope. Netherfield's housekeeper had been instructed to prepare for her master's arrival. He would come within a day or two and remain several weeks for the shooting. Mrs. Bennet could scarcely contain her restlessness, alternately looking at Jane, smiling, and shaking her head.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming, sister”—for Mrs. Philips had first brought the report. “Well, so much the better. Not that it matters to me, of course. He is nothing to us, you know, and I certainly have no wish ever to see him again. Still, he is perfectly welcome to visit Netherfield if he chooses.

“But in fact, once we rise to a certain height, the weight of air we pass through as we climb farther does not increase in proportion to the extra distance. As the earlier explanation shows, that proportion steadily decreases. It therefore seems clear that, however high we rise, we cannot literally reach a point beyond which no atmosphere remains. Some air must still exist, I argued, even if it has become infinitely thin.

“I knew, of course, that people had offered arguments for a definite boundary to the atmosphere, with absolutely no air beyond it. But those who supported this idea had overlooked something. It did not prove them wrong, yet it seemed to deserve careful study. Consider the time between each visit of Encke's comet to the point in its orbit closest to the sun. Even after allowing as accurately as possible for all the changes caused by the planets' gravitational pull, these intervals appear to be growing shorter. This means that the longest dimension of the comet's oval orbit is slowly but steadily shrinking. That is exactly what we would expect if an extremely thin substance, or ether, filled the region of its orbit and resisted its movement. By slowing the comet, this substance would weaken the force carrying it outward and strengthen the force drawing it inward. In other words, the sun's pull would gain more influence, bringing the comet closer with each circuit. Indeed, there is no other way to explain the change. There is another observation, too. The actual width of the cloud surrounding this comet shrinks rapidly as it nears the sun, then expands just as quickly as it heads towards the farthest point of its orbit. Wasn't I justified in agreeing with M. Valz that this apparent reduction in size was caused by pressure from the same ether I had described? That substance would simply become denser the closer it was to the sun. The lens-shaped glow known as the zodiacal light also deserved consideration. This light, especially clear in the tropics and impossible to mistake for a meteor's glow, stretches diagonally upward from the horizon. It generally follows the direction of the sun's equator. To me, it clearly seemed to be a thin atmosphere extending outward from the sun, reaching at least beyond Venus's orbit and, I believed, indefinitely farther. I could not imagine that this substance was limited to the comet's oval path or to the area immediately around the sun.
